name: Aero
lede: Aero is a clear, slightly grayed light blue that Maerz and Paul's 1930 color dictionary filed in 1920 as a textile-trade name, not, as the word's shape suggests, a nod to aviation.

sections.title: A name in the trade, not the sky
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary dates Aero to 1920, plate 36, swatch H 6, and gives its origin in three words: a textile-trade name [1]. That is a specific, sourced answer, and it rules out the obvious guess: 1920 is early for "aero-" to mean air travel in popular use, and the dictionary does not connect the word to flight at all [1]. The exact product or trade the name served is undocumented in the sources consulted here [1].

The 1955 ISCC-NBS dictionary filed the exact name Aero under block 186, "grayish blue" [2], while our own graph's computed-nearest ISCC-NBS block for this exact hex is a neighboring one, block 181, "light blue" [3] — the real 1955 filing and the nearest-block computation land one neighborhood apart, which happens when a named color sits near a block boundary. Munsell gives 2.2PB 7.2/7.7, a pale, moderately saturated blue [1]. The hex #7CB9E8 is a screen approximation; it is also a CSS Level 4 color keyword [1]. On a painter's color wheel its rotated complement lands near [[tan]], [[cinnamon-buff]] and [[sandstone]] — the warm, sandy opposite of a cool, pale sky blue [9].

sections.title: Its neighbors
sections.body: In the color graph, Aero's closest neighbor is [[squill-blue]], 3.4 units away and almost the same color [4]. [[french-sky-blue]] sits 4.1 units off, purpler and more vivid; [[blue-jeans]] is 4.5 units off, more vivid and darker; the basic term [[sky]] is also 4.5 away, and lighter [4]. [[iceberg]], 5.4 units off, is darker, and [[pale-cerulean]], 5.5 off, is duller and lighter [4]. None of these six distances is small enough to call the same color as Aero, so it occupies its own small patch of pale, grayish blue rather than duplicating a neighbor [4].

sections.title: Seen in
sections.body: Pantone named a close cousin of this blue, Cerulean, its Color of the Year for 2000, 6.7 units from Aero [5]. Denim's first light-wash workwear blues land 9.1 units off, close enough to share a family resemblance but clearly a different cast [5]. Among design aesthetics, the closest full-palette matches are [[look:space-age|Space Age]], 1.2 units off on Aero itself, and [[look:minimalism|Minimalism]], 1.9 off, with [[look:brutalism|Brutalism]] a step further at 2.2 units on its neighbor Squill Blue [6]. On screen, the 2023 film [[film:barbie|Barbie]] carries a painted-sky blue 5.1 units from Aero, and the Pixar color-scripts tradition for soft pastel skies sits 7.6 units off [7].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds this blue in 25 of 23,778 paintings, about 0.11 percent as photographed; a stricter within-painting lens finds it in 17 [8]. That makes it rarer than 64 percent of the named colors in the archive [8]. Inside a painting it most often sits as a mid-tone, in 35 percent of its 17 clearest matches, ranked by lightness within each canvas so an aged varnish cannot fake the result [8].

The earliest match is Michelangelo's work from 1500, with the third-earliest dated to 1617 and the latest to 1926, 20 dated paintings in all [8]. The archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor, not a first; a 1500 match is 420 years before the name's own 1920 record, so it is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof that anyone called it Aero, or made a matching dye, that early [8]. The 1800s carry the strongest later lift, 1.3 times the expected rate among 8,344 paintings from that century [8]. In printed English the adjective sense of the word itself peaks in the 1940s, two decades after the dictionary's 1920 record [8]. This is a computed color match on photographed, varnished canvases, not a pigment test.

questions.q: What does Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary say Aero's name actually comes from?
True or false: the real 1955 ISCC-NBS filing for the name "Aero" and our own computed-nearest ISCC-NBS block for its hex name the same category.
Why can Aero appear in a Michelangelo-era painting from 1500, four centuries before the name existed?
choices: The color match is on the painting's blue, not on who named it first
The painting was repainted in the 1920s
The archive only includes paintings after 1920
questions.answer: The color match is on the painting's blue, not on who named it first

openers: Aero reads like an aviation word, but the 1930 dictionary that first recorded it in 1920 calls it a textile-trade name instead.
Our own computed-nearest ISCC-NBS block for Aero's hex, and the real 1955 filing for the name Aero, land in two different neighborhoods of grayish blue.
